title: Distributed Acoustic Sensing for Urban Monitoring: Coverage Thresholds and Percolation
abstract: Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) enables the repurposing of existing fiber-optic networks as ultra-dense, long-range seismic arrays for urban monitoring. However, constraints imposed by real-world fiber infrastructure topology and components limit its use for city-scale applications. Recent technological developments have paved the way for short-range, on-chip DAS. Assuming their availability, and based on a Graph Theory framework, we show that monitoring applications fall along a coverage spectrum with two critical thresholds that define three distinct regimes. Low coverage (<10%) can, with optimal design, resolve earthquake early warning, groundwater monitoring, geological mapping, and urban activity tracking. A percolation transition occurs at 51.6% coverage, beyond which the city effectively becomes fully covered and statistical traffic monitoring is possible. Only for effectively complete coverage, infrastructure monitoring, individual vehicle tracking, and pedestrian movement analysis become possible. Thus, privacy-related risks remain very low. We show and exemplify how, for metropolises around the world, an optimal sensing network can be designed for earthquake early warning, traffic monitoring, and urban activity tracking. This framework provides a near-future roadmap for deploying urban DAS networks as a backbone of smart city sensing.
summary: This paper develops a theoretical framework using graph theory and percolation concepts to assess how well urban areas can be monitored using existing fiber-optic infrastructure via Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS). It determines critical coverage thresholds, notably $51.6\%$, that dictate the transition from localized monitoring capabilities to full city-scale network connectivity for applications like traffic tracking or early warning systems.
main_problem: Analyzing the potential of Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) for city-scale urban monitoring given constraints from real-world fiber infrastructure topology.
main_result: The analysis identifies three distinct operational regimes based on coverage: low, transition ($\approx 51.6\%$ percolation), and high coverage, providing a roadmap for smart city deployment.
method: Graph Theory and Percolation Theory are used to model the urban street network connectivity as a planar graph subjected to varying levels of sensor coverage.
model_or_system: The physical system is an existing fiber-optic network repurposed into ultra-dense seismic arrays (DAS), modeled mathematically as a planar graph $G(V, E)$ representing city streets. The analysis uses bond percolation theory on this graph structure.
key_observables: Coverage Ratio ($c$), Largest Connected Component Size ($S_{max}$), Percolation Threshold ($c^\star$).
important_parameters: Critical coverage ratio $c_\star \approx 51.6\%$; sensing range (e.g., 500 m); minimum required sensor separation ($D$); population density ($ho$).
main_assumptions: Availability of short-range, on-chip DAS technology; the city map can be accurately modeled as a planar graph; specific optimization goals (EEW, traffic) define placement strategies.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic sensing principles in Tel Aviv and show quantitative results regarding critical distance vs. coverage ratio, highlighting the percolation transition point at $c_\star \approx 51.6\%$.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the DAS platform, models the urban map as a graph, applies percolation theory to define connectivity thresholds ($c^\star$), and then develops optimization frameworks for specific applications (EEW, traffic) based on these coverage regimes.
why_interesting: While applied to civil engineering/geophysics, the core mathematical framework—using percolation theory to define phase transitions in a complex network structure—is highly relevant to understanding connectivity thresholds in quantum networks or disordered physical systems.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
